name: BURGER SHE GOAT (comes with goat cheese)

recipe.history:
Goat cheese — fromage de chèvre in French — is among the oldest cheeses on earth, predating cow's milk cheese by thousands of years. Goats were among the first animals domesticated by humans, with archaeological evidence of goat herding in the Zagros Mountains of present-day Iran dating back approximately ten thousand years. Goats thrive in rocky, arid terrain where cattle cannot survive, and so goat husbandry spread across the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East, and North Africa, becoming foundational to the food cultures of Greece, southern France, Spain, the Levant, and sub-Saharan Africa. The cheese produced from goat's milk — white, fresh chèvre, aged crottin, log-shaped Sainte-Maure de Touraine, crumbled Greek feta (traditionally made from a blend of sheep and goat milk) — developed independently across dozens of traditions, each shaped by local microclimates, terroir, and technique. Fresh chèvre, the bright-white, creamy, tangy variety most familiar to Americans, is a product of the Loire Valley of France, where the chalky limestone soils and temperate climate produce the specific flora that goats graze on, imparting the cheese with its characteristic lemony tang and earthy depth. The Loire has been producing chèvre for at least a thousand years; legend connects the region's tradition of goat cheese to the Moorish invasion of the 8th century, when Moorish armies, defeated at the Battle of Tours in 732, retreated and left behind their goat herds.

Goat cheese arrived in American culinary consciousness largely through the work of California cheesemakers in the 1970s and 1980s. Laura Chenel, a pioneering dairy farmer in Sonoma County, began producing fresh chèvre in the late 1970s after studying in France, and her cheese caught the attention of Alice Waters at Chez Panisse in Berkeley, who put goat cheese salad on the menu in the early 1980s. This single act — a warm chèvre salad with walnuts, beets, and frisée — helped reshape American restaurant culture's relationship with cheese, signaling that domestic artisan cheesemakers could produce world-class product. Through the 1990s and 2000s, American goat cheese production exploded, with small dairies across the country producing fresh chèvre, aged logs, and washed-rind varieties. Goat cheese on a burger was perhaps inevitable: its tang cuts through beef fat, its creaminess provides richness without the heaviness of American or cheddar, and its bright, slightly earthy flavor elevates the whole composition. This burger uses both fresh chèvre and a crumbled aged goat cheese, honoring the full spectrum of the tradition.

I grew up in a household that did not eat goat cheese, partly for reasons of familiarity and partly because my father found the aroma challenging. My first encounter with it was at a food market in my early twenties, where a vendor was giving out samples of fresh chèvre on small crackers drizzled with honey. I expected something overwhelming and found instead something delicate, tangy, slightly earthy, and rich in a way that was entirely different from cow's milk cheese. I went home and looked up every recipe I could find that used it. Over the following months I worked my way through the canon: beet and goat cheese salad, goat cheese and fig crostini, goat cheese tarts, goat cheese stuffed into chicken breasts. Eventually I put it on a burger and realized that I had been overthinking it. The burger was the right vehicle all along. The warmth of the patty softens the chèvre into a nearly molten state; the tang interacts with the beef's savory depth; the slight sweetness from caramelized onion or honey brings everything into balance. It is a simple, almost obvious combination that somehow feels like a discovery every time.

Goat cheese is at its best when the heat around it is controlled and intentional, which is one more reason to cook the patty it accompanies to medium rare — 130–135°F. At that temperature, the patty is hot enough to begin melting and softening the chèvre placed on top during the final minute of cooking, but not so blazingly hot that it destroys the cheese's delicate lactic structure. A well-done patty runs hotter and can cause the goat cheese to break and become greasy rather than creamy. Medium rare provides the gentle, sustained warmth that coaxes the cheese into its ideal state: soft, slightly oozing, still holding its form while yielding to the touch. This is the same principle that governs the cooking of any composed dish — every element should be treated at the temperature that is ideal for it, and medium rare is the temperature ideal for both the beef and, consequentially, for everything it touches.
ingredients: For the aged goat cheese crumbles:
3 oz aged goat cheese (crottin or aged chèvre), crumbled
6 fresh figs, stems removed and quartered (or ½ cup dried figs, soaked in hot water 20 minutes and drained)
1 cup mixed fresh herbs and greens: baby arugula, fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves, fresh basil leaves, fresh mint leaves
¼ cup walnuts, toasted and finely chopped
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Dissolve yeast in warm water with sugar. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine both flours and salt. Add yeast mixture and olive oil. Knead on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1–1½ hours until doubled.

2. Divide dough into 6 portions, shape into smooth balls, and set on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 400°F. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Score the top of each bun with a single shallow slash using a sharp knife or razor. Bake 18–20 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

3. Make the chèvre schmear: Beat chèvre with heavy cream until smooth and spreadable. Stir in thyme, lemon zest, honey, pepper, and salt. Taste and adjust — it should be tangy, lightly sweet, and herby. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Make the caramelized fig jam: Melt butter in a small skillet over medium heat. Add figs and cook 3–4 minutes until softened. Add balsamic vinegar, honey, and thyme. Cook, stirring frequently, until the liquid reduces and the figs become jammy and glossy, about 5–7 minutes. Season with salt. Cool to room temperature.

5. Make the walnut-rosemary oil: Combine toasted walnuts, olive oil, minced rosemary, and grated garlic in a small bowl. Stir to combine. Season with salt. Let sit at least 15 minutes for flavors to meld.
6. Make the herb salad: Just before assembly, toss arugula, parsley, basil, and mint with olive oil, lemon juice, and a pinch of salt. Dress lightly — the herbs should be barely coated.
7. Form patties: Gently combine ground beef with salt, pepper, and dried thyme. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Form into ¾-inch-thick patties with a center dimple.

8. Cook patties: Heat a cast iron skillet or flat-top over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip. In the last 90 seconds of cooking, crumble aged goat cheese over each patty and add a small spoonful of chèvre on top. The warmth of the patty will soften both cheeses. Cook until internal temperature reaches 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove and rest 3 minutes.
9. Toast buns: Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat and toast buns cut-side down 2–3 minutes until golden.
10. If using prosciutto: Briefly warm slices in the pan used for the patties, 30 seconds per side.

11. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of chèvre schmear on the bottom bun. Place the medium rare patty with melted goat cheeses on the bottom bun. Add a spoonful of fig jam alongside or on top of the cheese. Lay prosciutto over the top if using. Add the herb salad. Drizzle with walnut-rosemary oil and a thin thread of honey. Finish with flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun (spread with a thin layer of chèvre schmear on the inside) and serve immediately.
